Issued at 130 PM CST Thu Nov 19 2026

REST OF THIS AFTERNOON - TONIGHT:

Early this afternoon, surface low pressure is centered over 
northwest Ontario, but is quickly exiting to the northeast. 
Regional radar imagery does occasionally show some weak 
precipitation echoes aloft, but limited moisture return has kept
much of this precipitation from reaching the ground. Still, 
expect brief light rain showers or sprinkles to continue at 
times this afternoon into mid-evening primarily for the Iron 
Range into tip of the Arrowhead and areas north. Very little, if
any rain accumulation is expected.

Outside of precipitation, temperatures remain mild today with 
highs in the 40s in northeast Minnesota where skies have 
remained cloudy and low/mid 50s in northwest Wisconsin where 
there has been some sunshine. Strong, gusty southwest winds 
persist through the afternoon before gradually becoming westerly
this evening as they rapidly weaken. Expect calm to light and 
variable winds tonight as mostly cloudy skies continue with low 
temperatures in the low to mid 30s. Can't rule out some patchy 
fog tonight, but the combination of cloud cover and possibility 
for winds to not go completely calm could limit fog potential. 

FRIDAY - THIS WEEKEND:

The trend in precipitation for this weekend has not shifted too
much from the forecast this morning. A longer wave trough over 
the western CONUS slides east through the Upper Midwest later 
Saturday and Sunday. At the surface, this will spin up low 
pressure in the lee of the Rockies of Wyoming tonight/early 
Friday and eject it northeastward through the Dakotas and 
northwestern Minnesota. Both AI and physics-based ensembles are 
in good agreement on the low pressure center to track through 
northwestern Minnesota, largely staying northwest of or barely 
passing through Koochiching County. While strong warm air 
advection with this system will keep temperatures very 
seasonably warm on Friday (highs in the mid 50s to low 60s), the
moisture return quality and synoptic forcing for lift in the 
Northland will be slightly displaced from one another. 
Therefore, the best precipitation signal would be north and west
of the low center, keeping higher precipitation amounts mainly 
northwest of the Northland on Friday into Friday night. There 
should be some light rain showers associated with isentropic 
ascent and the warm front daytime Friday into Friday night, 
mainly in northern Minnesota. There should be a brief lull in 
precipitation before another round of rain develops ahead of and
along a cold front as it moves east through the area. The best 
chances for light rain with this second round of precipitation 
would be from the I-35 corridor into the tip of the Arrowhead 
and east into northwest Wisconsin. 

Precipitation associated with the cold front exits east of the 
Northland Saturday night, though colder air wrapping around on 
the back side of the departing low-pressure system will lead to 
the warmest temperatures of Sunday occurring around or shortly 
after midnight Saturday night and then gradually dropping 
throughout the day. This, combined with light, cold-advection 
showers should lead to any remnant precipitation on Sunday 
gradually transitioning from light rain to a rain/snow mix to 
all light snow. This snow ends for most of the area Sunday 
evening, but light lake-effect snow if forecast to linger into 
early Monday morning for the South Shore lake-effect snowbelts 
before drier air wins out.

Rainfall and liquid-equivalent precipitation amounts remain 
light. There is a 30 to 50% chance for at least one-quarter inch
near the Canadian Border, though totals of less than one- 
quarter of an inch are currently favored there. In northwest 
Wisconsin, there is a 50 to 70% chance for totals of at least 
one-quarter inch, mainly east of a line from Spooner to 
Ironwood.

Snow accumulation with this system also appears light and 
relegated mainly to areas north of the Iron Range and in the tip
of the Arrowhead, as well as parts of the South Shore lake- 
effect snowbelts. The probabilities for one inch or more of snow
in these locations remains at 20-40%.

EARLY TO MIDDLE OF NEXT WEEK:

More seasonable weather and a largely drier pattern sets up for
the first half of the next work week as high pressure slides 
through the Upper Midwest and Great Lakes. Expect high 
temperatures in the upper 20s to mid 30s and lows in the 10-low 
20s range from Monday through Wednesday. Some troughing aloft on
the backside of the high pressure Tuesday night into Wednesday 
could bring light snow chances back to the Northland, but 
confidence is low as global ensembles still show a large amount 
of variability with regards to precipitation potential and 
available moisture as this feature moves through. Therefore, we 
have kept precipitation probabilities low at less than 20%.
